title: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer
gist: UNEP's latest report concedes for the first time that keeping warming below 1.5C is no longer viable and sets a minimal-overshoot pathway needing 320 Gt of carbon removal, 70 percent emissions cuts by 2040 and coal phase-out by 2040, while current pledges cut only about 12 percent by 2035 and policies point to 2.8C by 2100.

insights.claim: For the first time, the UN Environment Programme acknowledged that keeping warming below 1.5C is no longer viable and shifted its goalposts to minimizing the duration and magnitude of overshoot.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Policy framing is moving from avoiding to managing overshoot, shifting emphasis toward carbon removal.
insights.quote: Decades of insufficient climate action makes exceedance of 1.5° C unavoidable

insights.claim: A strong El Niño will almost certainly push temperatures over 1.5C regardless of which record is used, though the UN's multi-decade averaging means the limit is technically not yet crossed.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Near-term record temperatures will intensify pressure for policy response.

insights.claim: Existing policies would leave the world about 2.8C above preindustrial by 2100, stretch Paris goals would cut that by just 0.2C, and adding all net-zero pledges outside Paris would still yield 2.1C.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Even full pledge delivery leaves large warming, so adaptation and removal demand grows.

insights.claim: Emissions were largely flat between 2024 and 2025, with fossil fuel emissions actually up and offset by better land-use management, when they needed to already be falling.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: No emissions peak yet means carbon-intensive demand persists.
insights.locator: And we don’t seem to be closer

insights.claim: The gap between policies and targets would look worse had the US not left the Paris process, as the Trump administration pulled out of the agreement a second time.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: US withdrawal removes the largest historical emitter from accountability.
insights.locator: The Paris Agreement’s means of getting to that goal

insights.claim: UNEP's scenario gives a 66 percent chance of capping warming at 1.8C and even odds of returning below 1.5C by 2100, requiring 320 gigatonnes of CO2 removal, roughly five years of present emissions.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Carbon removal is implicitly required at scale for a technology still in its infancy, a long-run demand signal for CDR.

insights.claim: The scenario requires cutting coal use for electricity by 75 percent by 2035 and phasing it out by 2040, cutting oil and gas by 30 and 35 percent by 2040, and dropping greenhouse gas emissions 70 percent by 2040.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Implied structural decline in fossil demand contrasts with projected oil and gas increases.
insights.locator: But that also has to be accompanied

insights.claim: Current pledges would cut emissions only about 12 percent by 2035, leaving 16 gigatonnes more CO2 emitted in 2035 than the minimal overshoot pathway; the gap is 5 gigatonnes for the 2C scenario.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Large pledge-to-need gap implies continued policy tightening risk.

insights.claim: Oil and gas demand is projected to rise for a decade or more rather than fall, and solar and wind are falling behind needed grid share because electricity demand is rising so quickly.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Demand growth is outpacing clean build-out, supporting continued fossil use near term.
insights.locator: There are failures across the board here.

insights.claim: The report was prepared before the conflict with Iran disrupted oil and gas supplies, so any conservation and electrification driven by shortages is not yet in the data.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Supply-shock-driven demand response is an unmodeled upside to electrification.

insights.claim: UNEP warns every added fraction of a degree and year above 1.5C raises the risk of irreversible changes in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation and coral systems.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Tail-risk framing underpins arguments for faster action.
insights.quote: Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5° C raises the risk of irreversible changes
